projects.title: Rentwise
projects.summary: A rental management app for small landlords: properties, tenants, agreements, deposits and rent collection with overdue alerts.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Landlords with a handful of units end up tracking rent, deposits and repairs across spreadsheets and chat threads, and overdue rent slips through.

sections.heading: What I built
sections.body: A React 18 + Vite app on the TanStack stack — Router for typed routes and search params, Query for data, Table for the payments ledger, Form for every form — backed by a small Node + SQLite server. A dashboard surfaces overdue and due-soon rent with WhatsApp/SMS reminders, occupancy, deposits held, open tickets and agreements ending.

sections.heading: Design choices
sections.body: All rent, deposit and finance rules live only in the server domain layer, enforced by a build-time layer check. The API is versioned at `/api/v1` with an OpenAPI contract, consistent error shapes and named actions like `/renew` and `/settle-deposit`, so future mobile apps can rely on it.

projects.title: Ledger Lite
projects.summary: A personal finance tracker that categorises spending automatically and explains where the money went.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Most budgeting apps make you do the boring part yourself. People gave up within a week because categorising transactions felt like homework.

sections.heading: What I built
sections.body: An import pipeline that reads bank statements, a rules engine plus a small model to categorise transactions, and a dashboard that answers one question well: where did my money go this month?

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: Trust matters more than accuracy. Showing *why* a transaction was categorised a certain way made people correct mistakes instead of abandoning the app.

projects.title: Trailhead
projects.summary: An onboarding flow that took new users from sign-up to their first success in under three minutes.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Half of new sign-ups never came back after day one. The product was powerful but the first screen asked too much.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body: We cut the sign-up form to two fields, added a guided first task, and ran weekly A/B tests to keep what worked.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: Activation jumped from 31% to 52% and support tickets about getting started dropped by a third.

projects.title: Pulseboard
projects.summary: A real-time status dashboard for internal services, with alerts people actually read.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: One screen for the health of every internal service, with grouped alerts so on-call engineers see the cause, not fifty symptoms.

posts.title: What a typed API layer actually bought us
posts.excerpt: We moved every endpoint behind generated types. Bugs went down, but the bigger win was how it changed code review.
body: Six months ago our frontend and backend agreed on data shapes the old-fashioned way: by hoping. This is what changed when we stopped hoping.
## The problem
Most of our production bugs weren't logic errors. They were **shape errors** — a field renamed on the server, an optional value treated as required, a date that was sometimes a string.
## What we did
- Generated TypeScript types from the API schema on every build
- Wrapped `fetch` in a tiny typed client so every call site is checked
- Made CI fail when the schema and the client disagree
## The surprising part
> The real win wasn't fewer bugs. It was reviews that talk about behaviour instead of field names.
Reviewers stopped asking “is this field nullable?” because the compiler already answered. Discussions moved up a level, to whether the feature made sense.

posts.title: Getting new users to “aha” in under three minutes
posts.excerpt: Notes from six weeks of onboarding experiments: what moved activation from 31% to 52%, and what didn’t.
body: Half of our sign-ups never came back after day one. Here’s what we tried, in the order we tried it.
## Cut the form
We went from seven sign-up fields to two. Everything else could be asked later, *in context*.
## One guided first task
Instead of a product tour, new users complete one small real task. Doing beats reading.
## Measure weekly, keep what works
- 12 experiments in 6 weeks
- 4 shipped, 8 thrown away
- Activation: 31% → 52%
> Most experiments fail. The process is what wins.

posts.title: Calm software
posts.excerpt: A short manifesto: software should load fast, say what it means, and never make you wonder what just happened.
body: I keep coming back to one test for anything I build: does it feel **calm**?
## Calm is fast
Every spinner is a small interruption. Speed isn’t a feature, it’s the absence of friction.
## Calm is honest
Buttons say what they do. Errors say how to fix them. Nothing pretends to work when it didn’t.
## Calm is predictable
The same action always does the same thing, in the same place.
> Good software feels obvious. That takes a lot of work.

about.headline: An engineer who never stopped tinkering.
paragraphs: I got into programming by automating chores nobody wanted to do. That habit stuck: I like finding the slow, annoying part of a system and making it disappear.
I work across the stack and I'm happiest on small teams where engineers talk directly to users — shipping, measuring, and iterating every week.
Away from the keyboard: long walks, filter coffee, and too many half-finished hardware projects.
